learner.profile: A technically curious learner of about twelve. An engineering lab with training wheels, not software for small children.
commitments: Short explanations immediately adjacent to something manipulable.
A visible cause-and-effect loop after almost every action.
Optional depth (goDeeper) rather than mandatory walls of text.
Authentic Sesame code, pins, protocols and numbers.
Meaningful choices aligned to the learning goal.
Debugging framed as normal engineering, never as failure.
Challenges unlocked by demonstrating a concept, never by a timer.
antiPatterns: No oversized cartoon buttons and no mascot narration.
No fake currency, points, gems or streaks.
No long forced walkthroughs: every step ends on a checkable observable, not on a Next button.
learner.antiPatternEnforcement: scripts/validate-lessons.mjs screens all prose for mascot, currency and celebration vocabulary, caps beginner12 explanation length, requires cause-and-effect coverage, requires every debug step to carry failureIsNormal, and rejects any success condition that is not one of the declared observable checks. There is no time-based or acknowledgement-based check type in the vocabulary, so a timer gate cannot be expressed.

meta.gateF: Every lesson claiming "this is how Sesame actually works" must cite a pinned firmware symbol or source location; if it cannot, it is labelled conceptual. In this file that rule lives on step.claim. type=factual with domain=firmware REQUIRES at least one symbol citation resolving in source-annotations.json. domain=library, domain=emulator and domain=lab are the three honest boundaries and each requires its own citation kind plus a boundaryNote. type=conceptual requires a conceptualReason and may not use "actually works" framing. Lesson-level grounding is COPIED from source-annotations.json curriculum[] and the validator fails if it differs, so a lesson cannot promote itself to factual.
meta.noHardwareClaims: Per docs/plan.md, "Standing constraint — no physical hardware, ever". No lesson in this file says a servo moved, a joint rotated or a pulse was observed. Angles are what the code COMMANDS. The pwm.output values here are recomputed from ESP32Servo 3.0.9 arithmetic and have never been observed at a pin: QEMU's LEDC model produces no waveform and there is no physical robot.
meta.curriculumOrdering: Not the research report's table order. Reordered around Sesame's real architecture, and around the report's own correction that movement sequencing must be taught before inverse kinematics because the firmware is sequence-oriented. The twelve factual modules run first; the seven conceptual ones close the curriculum, where "here is how Sesame works today, how could we improve it?" is a question the learner can answer.
meta.renodeDecision: The report's "Inside Renode" module is REWRITTEN as inside-qemu, not retired. Its subject — bus, memory, peripheral, time — is still worth teaching and the project has a working QEMU backend to teach it on; only the tool changed. The lesson keeps curriculumRef "inside-renode" so its grounding still resolves against source-annotations.json, carries supersedes: "inside-renode", and its final step tells the learner plainly that the original plan used Renode and why it was replaced.
consumers: The Phase 2 lesson runner (a later task): reads lessons[].steps[] in order, renders explanation at the learner's chosen level, binds manipulate.control, and evaluates success.check against robot/telemetry state.
The source explorer: links[].symbols and every symbol citation carry file/startLine/endLine already resolved.
The architecture graph and See-the-Signal: links[].concepts and links[].traceLayers are the cross-highlighting keys.
Lab mode: labHandoff names what each lesson leaves behind as an editable project.

lessons.title: Meet Sesame
lessons.learningGoal: Name the four things that make Sesame a robot - one controller, eight servo channels, one 128x64 display and the firmware that ties them together - and call any joint by the name the firmware uses for it.
willBeAbleTo: Point at any joint on the 3D robot and give its firmware name.
Explain why the joint order is R1, R2, L1, L2, R4, R3, L3, L4 and not alphabetical.
Say what the lab can and cannot tell you about a real robot.
lessons.labHandoff: The exploded view and the joint list stay available in Lab as the robot inspector.
openQuestions: The firmware never says which joint is a hip and which is a knee. Where would that information have to come from?

steps.title: Eight channels, eight names

explanation.beginner12: Sesame has eight joints. The code does not call them legs or arms. It calls them R1, R2, L1, L2, R4, R3, L3 and L4 - and that order is the order the firmware itself uses.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: A single `Servo servos[8]` array, indexed by an `enum ServoName`. The enum decides the numbering; nothing else does.
explanation.architecture: Eight PWM output channels on one microcontroller, addressed by index. Identity is the index; everything else is a label somebody added later.

goDeeper.title: Why that order looks scrambled
goDeeper.body: The enum is the wiring order, not a tour around the body. R4 comes before R3. Anything that re-sorts this list into something tidier is inventing an order the firmware does not have, and the two will disagree the first time you compare them.

citations.signature: enum ServoName : uint8_t { R1=0, R2=1, L1=2, L2=3, R4=4, R3=5, L3=6, L4=7 }

claim.text: The firmware declares exactly eight servo channels and names them with an enum, in the order R1, R2, L1, L2, R4, R3, L3, L4.

citations.signature: enum ServoName : uint8_t { R1=0, R2=1, L1=2, L2=3, R4=4, R3=5, L3=6, L4=7 }

manipulate.affordance: Rotate the robot, then pull the exploded view apart to separate the eight joint modules from the body.

expect.text: Each module you pull out is labelled with its firmware name, and the labels appear in enum order, not left-to-right.

observable.what: Eight labelled joint modules, in JOINT_ORDER.

success.description: Every one of the eight joints has been named correctly.
success.hint: The names are on the modules once you separate them. R and L are the two sides the firmware distinguishes; the digit is which of the four on that side.

steps.title: One wire per channel - and the wire depends on the board

explanation.beginner12: Each joint is driven by one pin on the controller. Sesame has been built on four different boards, and each board wires the same eight joints to different pins.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: A `const int servoPins[8]` array. Three of the four board pinouts are commented out; the Lolin S2 Mini one is live.
explanation.architecture: Logical channel to physical GPIO is a board-level binding. The channel identity survives a board change; the pin number does not.

claim.text: Four board pinouts are present in the source, three commented out. On the active Lolin S2 Mini profile the eight channels are on GPIO 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 13 and 14.

manipulate.affordance: Switch the board profile between s2-mini, distro-v3, distro-v2 and distro-v1 and watch the pin labels on the exploded robot.

expect.text: The pin numbers change on every joint. The joint names do not change at all.

observable.what: Pin labels update; joint names stay fixed.

success.description: A board switch was applied and the learner confirmed the joint names did not move with the pins.
success.hint: Compare R1 before and after. Its pin number is one of the things that changed. Its name is not.

steps.title: The face is a different device entirely

explanation.beginner12: Sesame's face is a small screen, and it is not wired like the joints at all. It has two wires instead of one, and it has an address.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: An `Adafruit_SSD1306 display` object, 128x64, on I2C address 0x3C, over the two pins the firmware defines as SDA and SCL.
explanation.architecture: A bus peripheral, not a GPIO output. One pair of wires is shared by every device on the bus, and each device is picked out by address.

claim.text: The display is a 128x64 SSD1306 on I2C address 0x3C, declared as a single object and driven over the two I2C pins the firmware defines.

manipulate.affordance: Click the OLED node in the architecture graph and follow it down to the two I2C pins.

expect.text: The OLED branch of the graph has an address on it. The servo branch has pin numbers and no addresses. That difference is the whole point.

observable.what: The graph highlights the OLED chain: display object, bus, pins.

success.description: The learner opened the source span that declares the display.
success.hint: Follow the OLED node down. The graph node links to the line of firmware that creates it.

steps.title: Run one real movement and watch eight names light up

explanation.beginner12: Press stand. Eight angles get sent, one per joint, in the same order you just learned. This is the whole robot doing its simplest job.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `runStandPose(1)` calls `setServoAngle()` eight times with fixed angles, then enters idle.
explanation.architecture: A pose is a vector of commanded angles applied in a fixed order. There is no solver anywhere in this path.

claim.text: runStandPose() commands the eight channels to a fixed vector of angles, in enum order, and every Sesame movement ends by calling it.

manipulate.affordance: Run the stand pose and watch the trace fill in.

expect.text: Eight servo.target rows appear, in JOINT_ORDER, carrying the angles written in the source you can see beside them.

observable.what: The movement announces itself with its own Serial banner.
Eight commanded angles, one per channel.
What the 3D scene ended up drawing.

success.description: All eight channels hold the angles runStandPose commands.
success.hint: Just run it. The check is that the eight commanded angles match the eight numbers in the source beside you.

steps.title: One row of that trace is not what it looks like

explanation.beginner12: Six rows appeared. Before you look closely: which of them do you think is a real measurement, and which is arithmetic somebody did for you?
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Every trace row carries a provenance badge. Read `pwm.output` and decide what its badge should say.
explanation.architecture: Provenance is a first-class property of a telemetry row. A system that cannot say where a number came from cannot be trusted about any of them.

claim.text: The pwm.output row is computed by this application. QEMU's LEDC model stores a duty value and produces no pulse, no edge and no waveform, and there is no physical robot in this project - so nothing has ever emitted the pulse that row describes.

citations.section: Standing constraint - no physical hardware, ever

claim.boundaryNote: This is a fact about the emulator and about this project, not about Sesame firmware. The firmware is innocent: it really does ask for that pulse.

manipulate.affordance: Open the pwm.output row and read its provenance badge and its witness line.

expect.text: The badge says the number was inferred for explanation. The witness line names the arithmetic and says no pin ever emitted it.

success.description: The learner identified pwm.output as computed rather than observed.
success.hint: Every row has a badge. Only some of them claim to have seen anything.

lessons.learningGoal: Follow one number all the way from the slider you moved to the pulse width the code asks for, and find the two places along that path where the number you asked for is not the number that arrives.
willBeAbleTo: Name the function every commanded angle in this firmware passes through.
Show two different requested angles that end up as one commanded angle, and explain which of subtrim and clamping did it.
Explain why a one-degree slider is over-promising.

openQuestions: setServoAngle() silently does nothing for channel 8. What would you have it do instead, and what would that cost?

steps.title: Every angle in this firmware goes through one function

explanation.beginner12: There is exactly one place in the whole program where an angle is handed to a joint. Find it once and you can follow every movement Sesame makes.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `void setServoAngle(uint8_t channel, int angle)` - seven lines, and every movement function calls it.
explanation.architecture: A single choke point between the movement layer and the driver library. That is what makes the rest of this lesson possible.

claim.text: setServoAngle(channel, angle) is the only function in this firmware that writes an angle to a servo channel.

manipulate.affordance: Drag R1 to 135 degrees - the angle the stand pose uses.

expect.text: One servo.target row appears for R1, and the source explorer highlights the same seven lines every time, whichever joint you drag.

observable.what: R1 commanded to the angle you chose.

success.description: R1 was commanded to 135 degrees.
success.hint: The slider is the control. 135 is the value the stand pose uses for this channel.

steps.title: Ask for channel 8 and predict what happens

explanation.beginner12: There are eight channels, numbered 0 to 7. What do you think happens if the code asks for channel 8? Commit to an answer, then try it.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: The whole body of setServoAngle() is wrapped in `if (channel < 8)`. There is no else, no return code and no log line.
explanation.architecture: A guard that fails silently. The caller cannot distinguish "done" from "ignored", so a mistake here is invisible until something does not move.

claim.text: setServoAngle() wraps its entire body in a channel < 8 guard and does nothing at all - no error, no log, no return value - for any channel outside that range.

citations.title: setServoAngle() silently ignores channels 8 and above

manipulate.affordance: Type channel 8 with any angle and send it.

expect.text: Nothing happens. Not an error - nothing. The trace stays empty, which is exactly what makes this kind of bug expensive.

success.description: A channel-8 command produced no servo.target event within the window.
success.hint: Watch the trace, not the robot. The evidence here is a row that never arrives.
success.failureIsNormal: Nothing you did was wrong. Silence is the observation.

steps.title: Subtrim is added BEFORE the limits are applied

explanation.beginner12: Sesame can nudge each joint by a fixed amount, to straighten a joint that sits crooked. The nudge is added first, and only then is the result squeezed back into 0 to 180. Order matters.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `constrain(angle + servoSubtrim[channel], 0, 180)` - one line, and the addition happens inside the constrain call.
explanation.architecture: A calibration offset applied upstream of saturation. Trim therefore consumes range at the ends rather than shifting the whole interval.

goDeeper.title: What the other order would have done
goDeeper.body: If the clamp came first and the offset second, a trimmed channel could be commanded past 180 and the library would have to deal with it. As written, the firmware can never ask for an angle outside 0-180 - but a channel with +40 of trim has lost the top 40 degrees of its range, and nothing tells you.

claim.text: setServoAngle() computes constrain(angle + servoSubtrim[channel], 0, 180): the per-channel offset is added first and the 0-180 clamp is applied to the result.

citations.title: Subtrim is added BEFORE the 0–180 clamp, so a large trim saturates the output

manipulate.affordance: Set R1 subtrim to +40, then command R1 to 160 and to 180 in turn.

expect.text: Both requests end up commanding 180. Two different numbers went in; one number came out. Nothing warns you.

observable.what: Both commands report the same commanded angle.

success.description: Two different requested angles were shown collapsing onto one commanded angle because of subtrim.
success.hint: 160 + 40 is 200, and 180 + 40 is 220. Both get squeezed to 180.
success.failureIsNormal: Finding this is the exercise, not a mistake. The firmware behaves this way on every robot that ships with it.

steps.title: The angle you asked for is not the angle at the pin

explanation.beginner12: You can type 181 different angles, from 0 to 180. Only 92 different pulses can actually come out. That means 89 of your angles are copies of the one next door.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Servo::write() maps 0-180 onto 732-2500 microseconds with integer map(), then usToTicks() truncates that into a 1024-step frame.
explanation.architecture: Two truncations in series against a 10-bit timer. The command resolution the API advertises is finer than the resolution the hardware timer can represent.

claim.text: Across the whole 0-180 range only 92 distinct pulse values are reachable, so 89 of the 181 commandable angles produce a pulse identical to their neighbour's. 99 and 100 degrees are one such pair: both become 87 ticks.

citations.note: The 10-bit timer width that causes the aliasing.

citations.text: int Servo::usToTicks(int usec) - usec / (REFRESH_USEC / timer_width_ticks), truncated to int

citations.title: 10-bit LEDC resolution means 89 of the 181 commandable angles alias onto a neighbour

claim.boundaryNote: This is arithmetic inside ESP32Servo 3.0.9, not inside Sesame source. Sesame only chooses the angle; the library decides what pulse that becomes. The numbers here are recomputed from the library's own formulas, not measured.

manipulate.affordance: Step the angle from 99 to 100 and watch the computed tick count.

expect.text: The requested pulse width changes. The tick count does not. At the pin those two angles would be the same request.

success.description: Two adjacent angles were shown producing the same tick count.
success.hint: Watch the ticks column, not the microseconds column. The microseconds are what was asked for; the ticks are what can be represented.

steps.title: Follow one number down all eight rungs

explanation.beginner12: One press, eight rows. Each row is a different thing being true, and two of them are guesses. Read the badges.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: The trace runs ui.command, http.request, firmware.command, movement.enter, servo.target, pwm.output, joint.target, visual.joint - in causal order.
explanation.architecture: A causal ladder with per-rung provenance. Each rung answers a different question and each has a different witness.

claim.text: On both backends the joint.target and pwm.output rungs are inferred, never observed. On the QEMU backend movement.enter and servo.target are observed from executing firmware; on the simulator they are produced by the behavioural model.
claim.boundaryNote: This describes what this project can witness. It is not a statement about Sesame hardware, which nothing here has ever touched.

manipulate.affordance: Run stand and open every rung of the trace in turn.

expect.text: Eight rungs, in order, each with a badge. The badges are not all the same, and that is the lesson.

observable.what: The command word and the function it names.

success.description: One command produced a row on every rung of the ladder.
success.hint: Any movement command will do it. Stand is the shortest.

steps.title: The last line of setServoAngle is stranger than it looks

explanation.beginner12: After every single angle, the code waits 20 milliseconds. But it does not sit still while it waits - it goes and does other jobs. You will take that apart properly later.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: The function ends with `delayWithFace(motorCurrentDelay)`, and `delayWithFace()` is a loop that services HTTP, DNS and the face animation every 5 ms.
explanation.architecture: Cooperative multitasking on a single thread. The delay is a scheduling point, not dead time.

claim.text: setServoAngle() ends by calling delayWithFace(motorCurrentDelay), and delayWithFace() spends that time calling updateAnimatedFace(), server.handleClient() and dnsServer.processNextRequest() in a loop.

citations.signature: int frameDelay = 100; int walkCycles = 10; int motorCurrentDelay = 20;

citations.title: delayWithFace() is not dead time — it pumps HTTP, DNS and the face animation

manipulate.affordance: Click through from the last line of setServoAngle into delayWithFace and read its six lines.

expect.text: You land in a while loop that is doing three other jobs. Nothing about the name suggested that.

success.description: The learner navigated from setServoAngle into delayWithFace.
success.hint: The call is on the last line of the function body.

success.description: One channel was commanded to all three angles.
success.hint: Any single channel. Watch the trace row change each time.

lessons.title: How PWM asks a servo to move
lessons.module: How PWM asks a servo to move
lessons.groundingNote: The 50 Hz frame, the pulse-range request and the 0–180 command range are Sesame source. The angle-to-pulse arithmetic and the 10-bit truncation are ESP32Servo 3.0.9, cited by library+version+line in TN-006 and TN-007 rather than by a firmware line. No pulse in this project has ever been observed on hardware.
lessons.learningGoal: Turn an angle into the pulse the code asks for, by hand and then with the inspector - and find the exact point where this project stops being able to tell you anything at all.
willBeAbleTo: Explain what a 50 Hz servo frame is and why the pulse width is the message.
Show that attach(pin, 732, 2929) never produces a 2929 microsecond pulse, and name the line that stops it.
Say precisely what QEMU does and does not do when the firmware writes to LEDC.
lessons.labHandoff: The pulse inspector becomes the Lab signal panel, wired to the same arithmetic.
openQuestions: The timer is 10 bits. If you could change one thing about this chain to get finer control, what would you change, and what would it cost?

steps.title: Fifty times a second, forever

explanation.beginner12: A hobby servo is not told "go to 90". It is told the same thing over and over, fifty times a second: a short pulse whose length is the message.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `servos[i].setPeriodHertz(50)` in setup(), then `attach()` per channel. The frame is 20 milliseconds long.
explanation.architecture: Position is encoded in pulse width on a fixed-period carrier. The carrier is a hardware timer; the width is the payload.

claim.text: The firmware sets every servo channel to a 50 Hz period in setup(), which is a 20 millisecond frame, and then attaches each channel to its pin.

manipulate.affordance: Set R1 to 90 degrees and read the frame: the pulse width and the gap that follows it.

expect.text: At 90 degrees the code asks for 1616 microseconds out of the 20000 microsecond frame - about 8.1 percent of it.

observable.what: The computed pulse width for the angle you set.

success.description: The learner read off the computed pulse and tick count for 90 degrees.
success.hint: The inspector shows three numbers: what was asked for, how many timer ticks that is, and what those ticks come back out as.

steps.title: The firmware asks for 2929. It never gets it.

explanation.beginner12: The code says the longest pulse should be 2929 microseconds. The library refuses, and quietly uses 2500 instead. Neither of them tells you.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `servos[i].attach(servoPins[i], 732, 2929)`. Inside Servo::attach(), `if (max > MAX_PULSE_WIDTH) max = MAX_PULSE_WIDTH;` runs before the value is stored.
explanation.architecture: A library-side saturation of a caller-supplied configuration value, applied silently at bind time. The caller keeps a wrong mental model for the life of the program.

claim.text: Both things are true: the firmware really does call attach(pin, 732, 2929), and ESP32Servo clamps the requested maximum to 2500 microseconds before storing it. The minimum is not clamped, because 732 is already above the library's own minimum. So the widest pulse this firmware can ever ask for is 2500.

citations.text: #define MAX_PULSE_WIDTH      2500     // the longest pulse sent to a servo
if (max > MAX_PULSE_WIDTH) max = MAX_PULSE_WIDTH;  - inside Servo::attach(), before this->max = max

citations.title: attach(pin, 732, 2929) never produces a 2929 µs pulse — the library clamps it to 2500

claim.boundaryNote: The clamp is in ESP32Servo 3.0.9. Reading only Sesame source would leave you believing in a 2929 microsecond pulse that cannot exist.

manipulate.affordance: Set the angle to 180 - the maximum - and compare the pulse the inspector reports to the 2929 in the source beside it.

expect.text: 180 degrees gives 2500 microseconds, not 2929. The source and the behaviour disagree, and the library is the reason.

success.description: The learner confirmed the maximum pulse is the clamped value, not the requested one.
success.hint: Set 180 and read the pulse. Then look at the third argument of the attach call in the source pane.
success.failureIsNormal: The firmware is not broken and neither are you. Two correct pieces of code disagree, and the library wins silently. Finding that is the job.

steps.title: Count how many pulses there really are

explanation.beginner12: Sweep all the way from 0 to 180 and count the different pulses. There are 92, not 181.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: 181 commandable angles map onto ticks 37 to 128 of a 1024-step frame. 89 of them collide with their neighbour.
explanation.architecture: Command-space resolution exceeding representation resolution. The excess is not an error; it is invisible, which is worse.

claim.text: Enumerating all 181 angles through ESP32Servo's own map() and usToTicks() yields 92 distinct tick values and 89 angles that alias onto a neighbour. This is a property of the library and the 10-bit timer, not of the emulator.

citations.title: 10-bit LEDC resolution means 89 of the 181 commandable angles alias onto a neighbour

claim.boundaryNote: Recomputed here from the library formulas and cross-checked against the same numbers derived independently in Q3. Nothing was measured.

manipulate.affordance: Sweep 0 to 180 and read the table of tick values. Look for the repeats.

expect.text: The tick column steps up unevenly. Some angles share a value with the one before; roughly every other angle does.

success.description: The full sweep was inspected and the aliasing counted.
success.hint: Count the rows where the tick number is the same as the row above.

steps.title: Where does this stop being something you can check?

explanation.beginner12: Everything so far was arithmetic, and arithmetic can be checked. The next step down - a real pulse on a real wire - is where this lab runs out. Predict what the emulator does with these numbers.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: QEMU's esp32 machine does model an LEDC device. It converts the duty to a percentage, stores one byte, and nothing ever reads it.
explanation.architecture: A register-accurate peripheral model with no signal generation. Register plausibility is not waveform correctness.

claim.text: QEMU's LEDC model has no timer, no clock, no GPIO connection and no output. Every servo write reaches it and is converted to a duty percentage that matches the TRM formula, and then it produces no pulse, no edge and no concept of 50 Hz. There is also no physical robot in this project, so nothing anywhere has emitted these pulses.

citations.section: Standing constraint - no physical hardware, ever

claim.boundaryNote: This is a fact about QEMU and about this project. Sesame firmware asks for the right pulse; nobody here can watch it arrive.

explanation.beginner12: The pulse row tells you a joint, an angle, a pulse and a tick count. It does not tell you which of the eight hardware channels carried it - because nobody here knows.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Eight LEDC channels are programmed and Q3 read back which eight. Which servo sits on which of them is not recorded anywhere in this repository.
explanation.architecture: A deliberate hole in the data model. The graph node states the set and declines to state the mapping.

claim.text: Q3 established which eight LEDC channels are programmed, but nothing in this repository records which servo is on which channel, so the trace prints no channel number at all.

citations.section: Section 1, "The edge the data does not support"

claim.boundaryNote: An absence, not a fact about Sesame. The honest move was to print nothing rather than a plausible guess.

lessons.learningGoal: Read a real Sesame movement as what it actually is - an ordered list of commanded angles and waits - predict where it ends up, and find the side effects that are not in the list.
willBeAbleTo: Predict the terminal pose of a movement by reading its source.

steps.title: A movement is a list, not a formula

explanation.beginner12: Sesame does not work out how to stand. Somebody wrote the eight angles down, in order, and the robot replays them. Every single movement in the firmware is like this.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Each movement is an `inline void run<Name>Pose()` in a header: a Serial banner, a face call, a run of setServoAngle() calls, some delayWithFace() waits, and a final runStandPose(1).
explanation.architecture: Open-loop scripted sequences. No kinematics, no interpolation, no feedback - which is exactly why sequencing is the right thing to teach first.

claim.text: The firmware contains 21 movement and pose functions, all hand-written as ordered calls. There is no movement data format and no solver anywhere in the tree.

citations.signature: prototypes for the nineteen movement functions

manipulate.affordance: Run stand with the source pane open, and watch the highlight walk down the function line by line.

expect.text: The highlight moves one line at a time, and one servo.target row appears per line. The list and the trace are the same thing.

observable.what: One row per source line, in source order.

success.description: All eight channels hold the angles runStandPose commands.
success.hint: Run it and compare the eight rows to the eight lines beside them.

steps.title: Wave names four joints. So why do all eight end up with new angles?

explanation.beginner12: Read the wave function and count the joints it names. There are 4: R1, L2, R4, L3. But run it and all eight get commanded. Work out why before you look.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: runWavePose() calls setServoAngle() on four channels itself - and calls runStandPose() twice, at the start and at the end, which commands all eight.
explanation.architecture: Direct effects versus transitive effects. A call graph question disguised as a robotics question.

claim.text: runWavePose() commands R1, L2, R4, L3 directly, and reaches all eight channels transitively because it calls runStandPose() at the start and again at the end.

manipulate.affordance: Run wave with the call graph open, and follow the calls out of the function body.

expect.text: Four joints are named in the source; eight appear in the trace. The extra four arrive from inside runStandPose.

observable.what: Rows from two different functions, interleaved.

success.description: The learner listed exactly the joints runWavePose's own body commands.
success.hint: Count only the setServoAngle calls written inside runWavePose itself. The rest come from a function it calls.

steps.title: The waits are part of the movement

explanation.beginner12: Wave repeats one arm motion four times, with a 300 millisecond wait each way. Change the wait and the movement feels different - but it still finishes in exactly the same place.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: A `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loop with `delayWithFace(300)` on each side. Change the delay and the terminal vector is unaffected.
explanation.architecture: Time is data in a scripted sequence. Duration and destination are independent, which is a property of open-loop replay.

claim.text: runWavePose() repeats one two-position arm motion four times with a wait on each side, and then commands the stand vector, so the terminal pose does not depend on the wait length.

manipulate.affordance: Copy wave into the editor, change the 300 ms waits, and run both versions.

expect.text: The shorter version finishes sooner and draws fewer face frames along the way. Both end on the same eight angles.

observable.what: The same commanded angles, closer together in time.

success.description: A timing change was applied and the terminal pose was shown to be unchanged.
success.hint: Compare the last eight rows of each run, not the whole trace.

steps.title: Stand is not just a pose - it is how the robot goes quiet

explanation.beginner12: Every movement ends by calling stand. And stand, when it is called the usual way, also puts the face into idle. That is why Sesame starts blinking on its own after a movement.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: runStandPose(int face = 1). With face == 1 it sets the stand face and calls enterIdle(); with face == 0 it only commands the eight angles. enterIdle() is reachable from nowhere else.
explanation.architecture: A shared exit path carrying a state-machine transition. The parameter is the difference between "go to this pose" and "finish".

goDeeper.title: The two calls inside wave are not the same call
goDeeper.body: runWavePose() calls runStandPose(0) at the start and runStandPose(1) at the end. The first is a pose change; the second is an ending. Same function, same eight angles, different meaning - and the only visible difference is the face.

claim.text: runStandPose() takes a face parameter defaulting to 1, and only the face == 1 path calls enterIdle(). enterIdle() sets the idle face in boomerang mode and schedules the next blink; nothing else in the firmware calls it.

citations.signature: void scheduleNextIdleBlink(unsigned long minMs, unsigned long maxMs)

citations.title: enterIdle() is reachable from exactly one place: runStandPose(face == 1)

manipulate.affordance: Run wave and keep watching after the last angle has been commanded.

expect.text: After the last commanded angle, the face becomes idle and then starts blinking at random intervals. Nothing asked for that; it fell out of the ending.

observable.what: WAVE, then the stand that ends it.

success.description: The face reached the idle state after the movement finished.
success.hint: Watch the face state, not the joints. It changes after the joints have stopped.

steps.title: Cancelling a walk runs a whole stand pose first

explanation.beginner12: Start walking, then send a different command. The walk does not just stop. It runs a complete stand pose - eight more angles - and then goes idle. That is what "stop" means here.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: The walk gait is punctuated by `pressingCheck(cmd, ms)`. If currentCommand has changed, it calls runStandPose(1) and returns false. The cancel path is a movement.
explanation.architecture: Cancellation implemented as a transition to a known pose rather than as an abort. Predictable, but it is not a no-op and it is not instant.

claim.text: pressingCheck() services HTTP, DNS and the face while it waits, and if currentCommand has changed it runs a full runStandPose(1) - eight commanded angles and an idle transition - before returning false.

citations.title: pressingCheck() cancels a walk by running a full stand pose, which enters idle

manipulate.affordance: Send forward, wait a moment, then send stand. Watch what arrives after the cancel.

expect.text: A complete stand pose appears in the trace after your second command - and then the idle face. The cancel cost eight commanded angles.

observable.what: Eight more rows, from the cancel path.

success.description: A mid-walk cancel was shown to produce a complete stand pose.
success.hint: Cancel it early, while the gait is still in its first cycle, so the stand rows are easy to pick out.
success.failureIsNormal: This is not a bug you caused. It is how the shipped cancel path works, and knowing it is the difference between predicting the robot and being surprised by it.

steps.title: Write a three-frame sequence of your own

explanation.beginner12: Now write one. Three positions, in order, with waits between them - and every angle has to stay inside 0 to 180 after subtrim is added.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Author it in the Lab sequence editor. The editor checks each commanded angle against the same constrain() the firmware applies.
explanation.architecture: Composing in the same shape the firmware uses. What you author here is a list, because that is what a Sesame movement is.

claim.text: The sequence editor is a Lab tool. This firmware has no movement data format and no way to receive a sequence at runtime - movements are C++ functions compiled into the image, which is exactly why Sesame Studio exists as a separate upstream tool.
claim.boundaryNote: What you author is a Lab artifact. It is shaped like a Sesame movement and it is validated against the same limits, but nothing here can send it to the firmware.

manipulate.affordance: Author three frames. Each frame is a set of commanded angles plus a wait.

expect.text: The editor rejects any angle that would be clamped, and shows you the commanded value beside the one you typed.

success.description: A three-frame sequence was authored with no out-of-range commanded angles.
success.hint: Check any channel that carries subtrim: the offset is added before the limit, so it eats your headroom.

steps.title: Where a solver would go - and why there is not one

explanation.beginner12: You could imagine telling Sesame "put this foot here" and letting it work out the angles. That is called inverse kinematics. Sesame does not do it, and to even ask the question you would need to know which joint is which leg - which nobody here does.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: A solver needs link lengths and a joint tree. The firmware has eight indices, eight names and eight pin numbers. It has no notion of a hip, a leg, or a left and right pairing.
explanation.architecture: The step from scripted sequences to kinematics is a step from an ordered list to a model. Sesame Robot Emulator has the list; it does not have a verifiable model.

claim.text: Sesame runs no kinematics of any kind. Describing a pose in terms of legs and hips is a reading laid on top of the firmware, not something the firmware says.
claim.conceptualReason: The firmware has no notion of a hip or a leg. It has eight indices and a name per index; which index is a hip, which limb a pair belongs to, and even left versus right are all semantic readings carried in hardware/joint-map.json with verified: false, and per docs/plan.md they can never be settled. Pose vectors are factual; the anatomy they are described with is not.

manipulate.affordance: Search the whole pinned tree for the words hip, leg, left and right. Count the hits.

expect.text: The movement functions name joints and angles and nothing else. There is no anatomy in the firmware to solve against.

observable.what: Angles, by channel. Never by limb.

success.description: The learner confirmed from the source that the firmware carries no limb naming.
success.hint: Read the eight lines. Every one of them names a channel, an angle, and nothing else.

steps.title: One list of names, expanded three different ways

explanation.beginner12: All of Sesame's face names live in one list. The compiler then reads that same list three times, and builds three different things out of it. Change the list once and all three change.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: An X-macro: `#define FACE_LIST X(walk) X(rest) ...`, expanded once into weak extern declarations, once into frame arrays, and once into the lookup table setFace() searches.
explanation.architecture: A single source of truth expanded by the preprocessor into declarations, storage and a registry. Adding a face is a one-line change by construction.

claim.text: FACE_LIST names 38 faces in one macro and is expanded three times: into weak extern bitmap declarations, into per-face frame arrays via MAKE_FACE_FRAMES, and into the faceEntries table that setFace() searches by name.

citations.signature: #define X(name) extern const unsigned char epd_bitmap_##name[] PROGMEM __attribute__((weak));

citations.title: The face list is one declaration expanded three ways by the preprocessor

manipulate.affordance: Open FACE_LIST, then follow it to each of its three expansions in turn.

expect.text: The same list of names shows up in three places that look nothing alike. None of them was typed out by hand.

observable.what: The face registry, highlighted in all three expansions.

success.description: The learner opened the FACE_LIST declaration.
success.hint: It is at the top of the bitmap header, above three thousand lines of image data.

steps.title: Pick a face by name

explanation.beginner12: Faces are chosen by name, not by number. The code looks the name up in the table, finds its picture frames, and draws the first one.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `setFace(const String&)` walks faceEntries, compares case-insensitively, sets currentFaceFrames and currentFaceFrameCount, and draws frame 0.
explanation.architecture: Name-keyed lookup into a static registry, with a fallback entry. The name is the API; the frame pointers are the implementation.

claim.text: setFace() looks the requested name up in faceEntries case-insensitively, counts its non-null frames, and draws frame 0 through updateFaceBitmap(), which clears the display, draws a 128x64 bitmap and pushes the buffer.

citations.signature: uint8_t countFrames(const unsigned char* const* frames, uint8_t maxFrames)

manipulate.affordance: Select the happy face and watch the virtual display.

expect.text: The display clears and one 128x64 frame is drawn. The reported face name matches what you asked for.

observable.what: A frame on the virtual OLED.

success.description: The happy face was selected and at least one frame was drawn.
success.hint: Any named face from the list. Happy is a good one to start with because it has frames.

steps.title: Ask for the stand face. Nothing happens.

explanation.beginner12: The firmware has a face called stand, and the stand pose asks for it. It draws nothing at all - and the robot does not notice. Your job is to work out why from the source.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: Every bitmap is declared weak and undefined. Two of them - stand and defualt - are never defined anywhere, so their frame arrays hold null pointers, countFrames() returns 0, and the fallback path selects the same empty array.
explanation.architecture: A weak symbol that nothing ever defines links successfully to a null address. The failure is silent by construction, and the fallback shares the defect.

goDeeper.title: Why nothing warned anybody
goDeeper.body: A weak declaration that is never defined resolves to null instead of failing the link. The Arduino platform compiles this sketch with warnings off, so there is no diagnostic at build time either. It was confirmed absent from the compiled ELF symbol table, so this is not something you can talk yourself out of by re-reading the source.

citations.signature: #define X(name) extern const unsigned char epd_bitmap_##name[] PROGMEM __attribute__((weak));

claim.text: The stand and defualt bitmaps are declared as weak externs and never defined, so countFrames() returns 0 for both. setFace("stand") therefore falls through to the fallback, which is the same empty array, sets currentFaceName to "default", and draws nothing - leaving whatever was on the display before.

citations.signature: #define X(name) extern const unsigned char epd_bitmap_##name[] PROGMEM __attribute__((weak));
uint8_t countFrames(const unsigned char* const* frames, uint8_t maxFrames)

citations.title: Two face bitmaps are declared but never defined, so those faces render nothing

manipulate.affordance: Select the stand face and watch both the display and the reported face name.

expect.text: The display does not change. The reported name comes back as "default", which is not what you asked for - and that mismatch is the only evidence you get.

observable.what: The previous frame is still on screen.

success.description: The learner observed the fallback: stand was requested, zero frames were drawn, and the reported face is "default".
success.hint: Compare the name you asked for with the name the robot reports afterwards. They are different, and that is the clue.
success.failureIsNormal: You have not broken anything. This is a real defect in the shipped firmware, tracked as ISSUE-20260823-004. Finding it from the source is exactly what debugging is.

steps.title: Ask for the same face twice

explanation.beginner12: Select a face. Now select the same face again. Predict what happens to the animation - does it start over?
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: setFace() early-returns when the requested name equals currentFaceName and the frame pointer is non-null. The frame index, the direction and the finished flag are all left alone.
explanation.architecture: An idempotence guard on a state setter. Cheap, correct for the common case, and surprising the one time you wanted a restart.

claim.text: setFace() returns immediately if the requested name matches currentFaceName and frames are already loaded, so re-selecting the current face does not reset the frame index and does not restart the animation.

citations.title: setFace() returns early when the name is unchanged, so a repeated call does not restart the animation

manipulate.affordance: Select the wave face, let it run partway, then select wave again.

expect.text: The animation carries on from where it was. Nothing restarts. To restart it you have to select something else and come back.

observable.what: Frame index continues rather than resetting.

success.description: The learner confirmed that re-selecting the current face does not restart its animation.
success.hint: Watch the frame counter, not the picture. It is the thing that would have reset.

steps.title: How a face plays is decided by whoever asked for it

explanation.beginner12: Some faces play once and stop. Some loop forever. Some bounce back and forth. That choice is not stored with the face - it is made by the line of code that selected it.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `setFaceWithMode(name, mode)` sets a single global currentFaceMode and then calls setFace(). Wave asks for its face in once mode; enterIdle() asks for idle in boomerang mode.
explanation.architecture: Playback policy held in global state and set per call site, rather than as a property of the animation. Two call sites can disagree about the same face.

claim.text: Playback mode is one global, set by setFaceMode() through setFaceWithMode() at each call site. runWavePose() selects its face in once mode; enterIdle() selects the idle face in boomerang mode.

citations.signature: void setFaceWithMode(const String& faceName, FaceAnimMode mode)
enum FaceAnimMode : uint8_t { FACE_ANIM_LOOP=0, FACE_ANIM_ONCE=1, FACE_ANIM_BOOMERANG=2 }

expect.text: The wave face plays through and stops. The idle face keeps going, bouncing forwards and backwards. Same mechanism, different mode.

observable.what: The call site that chose the mode.

steps.title: One function runs once. One runs forever.

explanation.beginner12: An Arduino program is two functions. setup() runs once when the robot powers on. loop() runs over and over, forever, until the power goes off. That is the whole program.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `void setup()` and `void loop()`. Everything else is called from one of them.
explanation.architecture: A bare-metal superloop. No scheduler, no threads, no operating system - so everything that appears concurrent is cooperative.

claim.text: setup() runs the 20-step boot sequence once, and loop() then runs forever, making six service calls before it looks at the current command.

manipulate.affordance: Open loop() and read it top to bottom. It is shorter than you expect.

expect.text: Six calls, then one long if/else chain, then the serial console. That is the entire runtime behaviour of the robot.

observable.what: The dispatch chain at the bottom of loop.

success.description: The learner opened loop().
success.hint: It is directly below setup(). Look for the six service calls at the top.

steps.title: Nineteen commands, one if/else chain

explanation.beginner12: When you press a button, the robot does not look anything up. It compares your word against nineteen others, in order, until one matches.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: A flat `if (cmd == "forward") ... else if (cmd == "backward") ...` chain over currentCommand, one branch per movement function.
explanation.architecture: Linear string dispatch. Order is the priority, and the command vocabulary is defined by this chain and nowhere else.

claim.text: The command dispatcher inside loop() is a flat if/else chain comparing currentCommand against 20 command words, each naming one movement function.

steps.title: A wait that does three other jobs

explanation.beginner12: Sesame has one processor and no way to do two things at once. So when a movement waits, it does not sit still - it answers the network, updates the face, and only then checks the clock again.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: `delayWithFace(ms)` loops until the deadline calling updateAnimatedFace(), server.handleClient() and dnsServer.processNextRequest(), with a 5 ms delay() between passes.
explanation.architecture: Cooperative multitasking without threads. Every servo write yields, because setServoAngle() ends with one of these.

goDeeper.title: This is also how a movement gets cancelled
goDeeper.body: server.handleClient() inside delayWithFace() can run an HTTP handler, and that handler can assign currentCommand. So the call stack really can be movement to delay to HTTP handler to a variable the movement is about to read. pressingCheck() reads exactly that variable. The re-entrancy is not incidental - it is the cancellation mechanism.

claim.text: delayWithFace() spends its wait calling updateAnimatedFace(), server.handleClient() and dnsServer.processNextRequest() in a loop, and setServoAngle() calls it after every single commanded angle - so a movement services the network between one joint and the next.

citations.title: delayWithFace() is not dead time — it pumps HTTP, DNS and the face animation

steps.title: The one failure that stops the robot completely

explanation.beginner12: Almost nothing in this firmware is fatal. Wi-Fi can fail, a face can be missing, a command can be nonsense - it keeps going. There is exactly one thing that stops it dead, and it is the screen.
explanation.beginnerProgrammer: If `display.begin()` returns false, setup() prints a line and executes `while (1);`. No servo is ever attached, because that happens later in setup().
explanation.architecture: A single unrecoverable initialisation. Ordering makes it worse: the display comes up before the servos, so a display fault takes the whole robot with it.

claim.text: A failed display.begin() is the only hard stop in this firmware: setup() prints "SSD1306 allocation failed." and enters while(1). Servo attach happens later in setup(), so nothing is ever attached and loop() is never reached.

citations.title: A failed display init is the only hard stop in setup()

expect.text: Boot stops at the display step. No servos are attached, no HTTP server starts, and loop() never runs. One line on the serial console is the entire diagnosis.

success.description: Boot was shown halting at the display step with the expected log line.
success.hint: Watch the boot step list. It stops, and everything after it never happens.
success.failureIsNormal: A halt is a legitimate design choice, not a bug. The exercise is deciding whether you agree with it - a robot that cannot show a face still has eight working joints.

steps.title: Send a word the robot does not know

explanation.beginnerProgrammer: The dispatcher matches nothing, so no branch clears currentCommand. Every subsequent loop() iteration walks the whole chain again and matches nothing again. /api/status keeps reporting it.
explanation.architecture: A state variable with no owner on the failure path. The self-clearing is written per branch, so a missing branch means no clearing at all.

claim.text: Only the branches that match clear currentCommand, and the continuous movement commands never clear it at all. An unrecognised word therefore stays in currentCommand indefinitely and is reported by /api/status on every request.

steps.title: A peripheral that stores the right number and does nothing with it

explanation.beginner12: The emulator does have a PWM peripheral. It works out the correct duty percentage, stores one byte, and nothing anywhere ever reads it again.

claim.text: QEMU's LEDC device is mapped and decoded, and every servo write reaches it and produces a duty percentage matching the TRM formula. It has no timer, no clock, no GPIO connection and no output, and the byte it stores has no readers in the binary.
claim.boundaryNote: This is what the emulator does, established by reading its registers back over a debugger. It is not a statement about Sesame or about any real chip.
